title: Usage
text: All the examples on this page show real results for the average day of May in Cuernavaca, Mexico (the EPW and materials.ini used here live in docs/data/ in the repository). The 1D examples are executed when the site is rendered; the 2D ones are pre-computed — a default-mesh 2D solve takes ~10–20 minutes — by docs/run_examples.py, whose outputs (in docs/data/results/) the page reads and plots. Regenerate them with uv run python docs/run_examples.py.

title: Usage
text:
Workflow
To simulate a wall (or roof) you need to:

Geolocate it — pass an EPW file to Location.
Orient it — set azimuth (and tilt if needed: 90 = wall, 0 = roof).
Define its color — set absortance.
Define its layers — set layers from outside to inside.
Choose the period — call location.meanDay(month, year).
Compute Tsa(), then choose one solver:

solve() — free-running: the indoor temperature Ti evolves with the dynamics of the constructive system.
solveAC() — air-conditioned: Ti is held at the comfort setpoint and the cooling/heating energies are reported.


Both solvers return pandas DataFrames indexed by time of day, on the same time grid as Tsa() — so results concatenate directly (pd.concat([data, wall.Tsa()], axis=1), no resampling, no NaN).

Tsa depends on absortance, tilt, azimuth, the month (meanDay) and the Location — it must be recomputed whenever any of these change.

title: Usage
text:
Recommended folder structure
materials.ini is required — EnerHabitat ships with no default materials.
project/
├── main.py
├── materials.ini      # Material properties (REQUIRED — user-provided)
└── epw/
    ├── ...
    └── example.epw

title: Usage
text:
Materials file
Material properties are declared in an .ini file: the material name is the section header and k, rho, c the keys (case-sensitive, no Greek letters). Inline comments (# or ;) are allowed. By default the package looks for materials.ini in the working directory; otherwise set eh.config.file.
The file below defines every material used in these docs, so you can run all the snippets as-is (values are typical/illustrative — replace with your own data):
[Adobe]
k   = 0.58    # Thermal conductivity, W/m·K
rho = 1500    # Density, kg/m³
c   = 1480    # Specific heat, J/kg·K

[Mortero]     ; cement mortar / render
k   = 0.70
rho = 1800
c   = 1000

[Ladrillo]    ; fired-clay brick
k   = 0.85
rho = 1600
c   = 840

[Concreto]    ; structural concrete (ribs, topping, hollow block)
k   = 1.80
rho = 2200
c   = 880

[Bovedilla]   ; lightweight filler block
k   = 0.50
rho = 1200
c   = 900

[Yeso]        ; gypsum plaster
k   = 0.37
rho = 900
c   = 1000

[EPS]         ; expanded polystyrene
k   = 0.04
rho = 15
c   = 1400

[Impermeabilizante]   ; asphaltic waterproofing membrane
k   = 0.17
rho = 1100
c   = 1000
If config.file points at a missing file, EnerHabitat reports Error: <path> not found and materials will be empty — solving then fails because the layer materials cannot be resolved.

title: Usage
text:
Examples
The examples form the system × mode matrix: 1D/2D, free-running and air-conditioned. Setup shared by all of them:

import enerhabitat as eh
import pandas as pd

eh.config.file = "data/materials.ini"
epw_file = "data/MEX_MOR_Cuernavaca-Matamoros.Intl.AP.767260_TMYx.2004-2018.epw"

Error: materials.ini not found




Plot helper used by the examples (click to show)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

EH_COLORS = {"Ti": "#2a78d6", "Tsa": "#eb6834", "Ta": "#008300", "Tn": "#6b7280"}
INK = "#374151"

def plot_day(df, cols=("Ta", "Tsa", "Ti"), title=""):
    """Temperatures of the average day, with the comfort zone Tn ± DeltaTn."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.6))
    hours = (df.index - df.index[0]).total_seconds() / 3600
    if "Tn" in df and "DeltaTn" in df:
        tn, dtn = float(df["Tn"].iloc[0]), float(df["DeltaTn"].iloc[0])
        ax.axhspan(tn - dtn, tn + dtn, color=EH_COLORS["Tn"], alpha=0.12, lw=0)
        ax.axhline(tn, color=EH_COLORS["Tn"], ls="--", lw=1)
        ax.annotate("comfort  Tn ± ΔTn", xy=(0.4, tn + dtn), va="bottom",
                    fontsize=8, color=INK)
    # end-of-line labels, dodged vertically if two lines end too close
    ends = {c: float(df[c].iloc[-1]) for c in cols}
    span = df[list(cols)].to_numpy()
    min_sep = 0.06 * (span.max() - span.min())
    ypos = dict(ends)
    order = sorted(cols, key=ends.get)
    for a, b in zip(order, order[1:]):
        if ypos[b] - ypos[a] < min_sep:
            ypos[b] = ypos[a] + min_sep
    for c in cols:
        ax.plot(hours, df[c], color=EH_COLORS[c], lw=2, label=c)
        ax.annotate(c, xy=(hours[-1] + 0.4, ypos[c]),
                    va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 26)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 6, 12, 18, 24])
    ax.set_xlabel("hour of the average day")
    ax.set_ylabel("temperature (°C)")
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25, lw=0.5)
    for s in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()



1D wall, free-running

wall = eh.System(eh.Location(epw_file))
wall.azimuth = 90                    # east-facing
wall.absortance = 0.3
wall.layers = [("Mortero", 0.025), ("Ladrillo", 0.10)]
wall.location.meanDay(month=5, year=2025)
wall.Tsa()

data = wall.solve()                  # free-running Ti
data = pd.concat([data, wall.Tsa()], axis=1)

print(f"energy_transfer = {wall.energy_transfer:,.0f} J/(m²·day)"
      f"  = {wall.energy_transfer/3600:,.0f} Wh/(m²·day)")

energy_transfer = 31,929 J/(m²·day)  = 9 Wh/(m²·day)



plot_day(data, title="Mortero + Ladrillo wall, east, free-running — May, Cuernavaca")








The indoor temperature Ti oscillates with a smaller amplitude than the sun–air temperature Tsa and lags behind it — the damping and the delay are the thermal mass at work.


1D wall, air-conditioned
Same wall; solveAC() holds Ti at the neutrality temperature Tn and reports the energy needed to do so:

dataAC = wall.solveAC()
dataAC = pd.concat([dataAC, wall.Tsa()], axis=1)

print(f"cooling_energy = {wall.cooling_energy:,.0f} J/(m²·day)"
      f"  = {wall.cooling_energy/3600:,.0f} Wh/(m²·day)")
print(f"heating_energy = {wall.heating_energy:,.0f} J/(m²·day)"
      f"  = {wall.heating_energy/3600:,.0f} Wh/(m²·day)")

cooling_energy = 968,152 J/(m²·day)  = 269 Wh/(m²·day)
heating_energy = 399,814 J/(m²·day)  = 111 Wh/(m²·day)



plot_day(dataAC, title="Same wall, air-conditioned (Ti = Tn) — May, Cuernavaca")










2D hollow-block wall, free-running
A concrete block with one air cavity per cell. The 2D element goes inside the layer stack; finishes are ordinary 1D layers around it.
block = eh.HollowBlock(
    material   = "Concreto",          # single material of the block
    emissivity = 0.9,                 # cavity-wall emissivity (radiation)
    geometry   = {                    # cell measures, in metres
        "web":          0.02,         # half web (rib) thickness
        "block_width":  0.16,         # cavity width
        "cover_top":    0.02,         # outer shell
        "cavity":       0.08,         # cavity height
        "cover_bottom": 0.02,         # inner shell
    },
)

wall2d = eh.System2D(eh.Location(epw_file))
wall2d.tilt = 90                      # walls only (required for HollowBlock)
wall2d.azimuth = 90
wall2d.absortance = 0.6
wall2d.layers = [("Mortero", 0.02), block, ("Yeso", 0.01)]

wall2d.location.meanDay(month=5, year=2025)
wall2d.Tsa()

ti = wall2d.solve()                   # free-running
print(wall2d.energy_transfer)         # J/(m²·day), per unit indoor area
Pre-computed result of that exact code:

import json

RES = "data/results"
summary = json.load(open(f"{RES}/summary.json"))

hollow = pd.read_csv(f"{RES}/hollow_free.csv", index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
s = summary["hollow_free"]
print(f"energy_transfer = {s['energy_transfer']:,.0f} J/(m²·day)"
      f"  ·  converged in {s['days']} days"
      f"  ·  solve time ≈ {s['runtime_s']/60:.0f} min")
plot_day(hollow, title="Hollow-block wall (2D), east, free-running — May, Cuernavaca")

energy_transfer = 47,705 J/(m²·day)  ·  converged in 4 days  ·  solve time ≈ 21 min











2D hollow-block wall, air-conditioned
wall2d.solveAC()                      # Ti held at Tn
print(wall2d.cooling_energy, wall2d.heating_energy)

hollowAC = pd.read_csv(f"{RES}/hollow_ac.csv", index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
s = summary["hollow_ac"]
print(f"cooling_energy = {s['cooling_energy']:,.0f} J/(m²·day)"
      f"  = {s['cooling_energy']/3600:,.0f} Wh/(m²·day)")
print(f"heating_energy = {s['heating_energy']:,.0f} J/(m²·day)"
      f"  = {s['heating_energy']/3600:,.0f} Wh/(m²·day)")
plot_day(hollowAC, title="Hollow-block wall (2D), air-conditioned — May, Cuernavaca")

cooling_energy = 1,611,252 J/(m²·day)  = 448 Wh/(m²·day)
heating_energy = 298,479 J/(m²·day)  = 83 Wh/(m²·day)











Joist-and-block roof (Slab)
Three solids (compression topping, L-shaped rib, filler block) plus N equal cavities that can be air (Fill.AIR) or a solid fill (Fill.SOLID).
slab = eh.Slab(
    rib_material     = "Concreto",       # joist/rib (L-shaped: web + foot)
    block_material   = "Bovedilla",      # filler block around the cavities
    topping_material = "Concreto",       # compression topping
    fill_type        = eh.Fill.AIR,      # or eh.Fill.SOLID (+ fill_material)
    emissivity       = 0.9,              # required if AIR
    geometry = {
        "web":          0.025,   # rib web
        "foot":         0.025,   # rib foot
        "shoulder":     0.050,   # block between rib and cavities
        "n_cavities":   3,
        "cavity_width": 0.103,
        "topping":      0.100,   # compression topping
        "topping_cap":  0.050,   # topping above the rib web
        "cover_top":    0.030,   # block above the cavity
        "cavity":       0.040,   # cavity height
        "cover_bottom": 0.030,   # block below the cavity
    },
)

roof = eh.System2D(eh.Location(epw_file))
roof.tilt = 0                            # roofs only (required for Slab)
roof.absortance = 0.3
roof.layers = [("Impermeabilizante", 0.003), slab, ("Yeso", 0.015)]
roof.location.meanDay(month=5, year=2025)
roof.Tsa()

roof.solve()                             # or roof.solveAC()

slab_df = pd.read_csv(f"{RES}/slab_free.csv", index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
s = summary["slab_free"]
print(f"energy_transfer = {s['energy_transfer']:,.0f} J/(m²·day)"
      f"  ·  converged in {s['days']} days")
plot_day(slab_df, title="Joist-and-block roof (2D), free-running — May, Cuernavaca")

energy_transfer = 27,041 J/(m²·day)  ·  converged in 5 days









Note how the roof’s Tsa drops below Ta at night: that is the long-wave radiation factor (\(RF = 3.9\) °C for horizontal surfaces) at work — the roof sees the cold sky (see the 1D model).


Filled cavities (Fill.SOLID)
The cavity of a HollowBlock (or the cavities of a Slab) can be filled with a solid material instead of air — e.g. an insulating core:
block = eh.HollowBlock(
    material      = "Concreto",
    fill_type     = eh.Fill.SOLID,
    fill_material = "EPS",
    geometry      = {"web": 0.02, "block_width": 0.16,
                     "cover_top": 0.02, "cavity": 0.08, "cover_bottom": 0.02},
)
Filling with the same material as the shell makes the unit homogeneous — equivalent to a 1D layer (this is one of the package’s validation checks).


Inspecting the section
Before solving you can inspect, to scale, how materials and node types are laid out on the 2D mesh:
wall2d.section_report()            # table: node types + materials (k, ρc, y-range)
wall2d.preview()                   # to-scale panels (node type, k, ρc)
wall2d.preview(field="materials", backend="ascii")   # terminal fallback
sec = wall2d.section()             # NT / k / rhoc arrays + mesh
matplotlib is an optional extra (pip install enerhabitat[viz]); without it the inspector falls back to a to-scale ASCII drawing.

title: Usage
text:
Configuration

config (global)
config is a global singleton shared by every Location and System. Changing it affects all subsequent computations.








Attribute
Default
Description




file
"materials.ini"
Path to the .ini file with material properties


La
2.5 m
Depth of the indoor air volume


Nx
200
Control volumes across the system thickness


ho
13 W/(m²·K)
Outdoor film coefficient


hi
8.6 W/(m²·K)
Indoor film coefficient


dt
10 s (fixed)
Time step — not configurable (assignments are ignored)



The ho/hi defaults are the values prescribed by the Mexican standards NOM-020-ENER and NOM-008-ENER; they can be overridden at any time. dt is locked because of the explicit indoor-air coupling — see the numerical method.
eh.config.file = "./materials.ini"
eh.config.La = 2.0
eh.config.ho = 12          # override the NOM defaults if needed
eh.config.reset()          # restore all defaults
config.materials is a read-only dict keyed by material name (eh.config.materials["Adobe"].k, .rho, .c).


config2d (2D mesh and convergence)
The physics (La, ho, hi, dt, air properties) is shared with config; config2d holds the 2D-only parameters:








Attribute
Default
Description

80
mesh nodes across the cell width (adiabatic sides)


ny
160
mesh nodes through the thickness (outside → inside)


tol_inner
1e-10
inner (line-by-line) loop tolerance


tol_day
5e-4
day-to-day convergence tolerance


max_days
60
cap on the day-to-day iterations



from enerhabitat import config2d
config2d.nx, config2d.ny = 120, 160

Each solve is single-threaded. For volume (many configurations), parallelise at the process level — run independent solve() calls in separate processes (multiprocessing, joblib); this scales near-linearly (≈6× at 8 processes). See Performance.

title: 1D model: physical problem
text:
EnerHabitat evaluates the thermal performance of a single opaque component of the building envelope — a wall or a roof. It considers that the only heat path into the indoor space is through the component under evaluation: there are no windows, no ventilation, no infiltration and no internal heat gains (Barrios et al. 2016). This makes results directly comparable across constructive systems: whatever difference appears in the indoor temperature or in the energy demand is caused by the constructive system alone.
The simulation runs over the average day of a chosen month, built from the EPW weather file (see The average day), and is iterated day after day until the solution becomes periodic — the daily cycle repeats itself. All reported results correspond to that converged, periodic day.

title: 1D model: physical problem
text:
Domain and assumptions
The constructive system is a stack of \(N\) homogeneous layers, ordered from outside (\(x = 0\)) to inside (\(x = L\)). Each layer \(j\) is described by three constant properties: thermal conductivity \(k_j\) (W/m·K), density \(\rho_j\) (kg/m³) and specific heat \(c_j\) (J/kg·K).






Figure 1: 1D domain: multilayer wall/roof with its boundary conditions and the indoor-air node.



The model assumes:

1D conduction perpendicular to the surface (the \(x\) direction); layers are homogeneous, so there is no in-plane heat flow.
Constant thermal properties per layer (no temperature dependence, no moisture).
Convective boundary conditions with fixed film coefficients \(h_o\) (outdoor) and \(h_i\) (indoor). The defaults, \(h_o = 13\) and \(h_i = 8.6\) W/m²·K, are the values prescribed by the Mexican standards NOM-020-ENER and NOM-008-ENER; both are configurable.
Solar and long-wave radiation on the outdoor surface enter through the sun–air temperature (Equation 4).
The indoor space is a lumped air node of depth \(L_a\) (2.5 m by default) in the free-running mode, or a fixed setpoint in the air-conditioned mode.

title: 1D model: physical problem
text:
Governing equations
Within each layer \(j\) the temperature field obeys the one-dimensional, time-dependent heat conduction equation (Incropera et al. 2007):
\[
\rho_j\, c_j\, \frac{\partial T_j}{\partial t} \;=\; k_j\, \frac{\partial^2 T_j}{\partial x^2},
\qquad j = 1, \dots, N,
\tag{1}\]
where \(t\) is time and \(x\) the coordinate perpendicular to the surface. At the joint between consecutive layers the temperature is continuous and the conductive flux is conserved:
\[
k_j \left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right|_{j,\,j+1}
\;=\;
k_{j+1} \left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right|_{j,\,j+1}.
\tag{2}\]

title: 1D model: physical problem
section: Outdoor boundary condition: the sun–air temperature
text:
Outdoor boundary condition: the sun–air temperature
At the outdoor surface, \(x = 0\), convection against the sun–air temperature \(T_{sa}\) balances the conducted flux:
\[
h_o \left( T_{sa} - T_{x=0} \right)
\;=\;
-\,k_1 \left.\frac{\partial T_1}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0}.
\tag{3}\]
\(T_{sa}\) is a fictitious temperature that lumps together the three thermal loads on the exterior surface — convection with outdoor air, absorbed short-wave solar radiation, and the long-wave radiative exchange with the sky (ASHRAE 1997):
\[
T_{sa} \;=\; T_a \;+\; \frac{a\, I_s}{h_o} \;-\; RF,
\tag{4}\]
where:

\(T_a\) — outdoor air temperature of the average day;
\(I_s\) — solar irradiance on the (tilted, oriented) surface, W/m²;
\(a\) — solar absorptance of the outdoor surface (the color of the wall/roof);
\(h_o\) — outdoor film coefficient;
\(RF\) — long-wave radiation factor: EnerHabitat uses \(RF = 3.9\ °\mathrm{C}\) for horizontal surfaces (tilt = 0, a roof facing the cold sky) and \(RF = 0\) for any other tilt (e.g. vertical walls, tilt = 90).

\(I_s\) is computed with pvlib (Holmgren et al. 2018) from the average-day beam, diffuse and global horizontal irradiances, the solar position at the site, and the surface tilt and azimuth. This is why Tsa() must be recomputed whenever the color, the orientation, the month or the location change.

title: 1D model: physical problem
section: Indoor boundary condition and solution modes
text:
Indoor boundary condition and solution modes
At the indoor surface, \(x = L\), the conducted flux is released by convection to the indoor air at temperature \(T_i\):
\[
-\,k_N \left.\frac{\partial T_N}{\partial x}\right|_{x=L}
\;=\;
h_i \left( T_{x=L} - T_i \right).
\tag{5}\]
What happens to \(T_i\) defines the two solution modes.

Free-running mode — solve()
The indoor air is a lumped thermal mass — density \(\rho_a\), specific heat \(c_a\), depth \(L_a\) — whose temperature evolves with the heat received from the indoor surface:
\[
L_a\, \rho_a\, c_a\, \frac{dT_i}{dt} \;=\; h_i \left( T_{x=L} - T_i \right),
\tag{6}\]
with \(L_a = 2.5\) m by default (config.La). The air properties are \(\rho_a \approx 1.18\) kg/m³ and \(c_a \approx 1005\) J/kg·K (config.AIR_DENSITY, config.AIR_HEAT_CAPACITY). Because Equation 6 is integrated in time alongside the wall, the time step is constrained by this coupling — see the numerical method for why config.dt is fixed at 10 s.
The reported energy_transfer is the heat delivered by the indoor surface to the air, accumulated over the converged day:
\[
E \;=\; \int_{24\,\mathrm{h}} h_i \left( T_{x=L} - T_i \right)^{+} dt
\qquad \left[\mathrm{J/(m^2\,day)}\right],
\tag{7}\]
where \((\,\cdot\,)^{+}\) keeps the positive part (heat entering the room). In the periodic regime the daily energy entering equals the energy leaving, so either one represents the transfer through the system.


Air-conditioned mode — solveAC()
The indoor air temperature is held constant at the neutrality temperature of the adaptive comfort model of Humphreys & Nicol (2000):
\[
T_i \;=\; T_n \;=\; 0.54\, \overline{T_a} \;+\; 13.5\ °\mathrm{C},
\tag{8}\]
where \(\overline{T_a}\) is the mean outdoor air temperature of the average day. The cooling and heating demands are the fluxes the air-conditioning system must remove or supply to keep \(T_i = T_n\):
\[
E_c \;=\; \int_{24\,\mathrm{h}} h_i \left( T_{x=L} - T_n \right)^{+} dt,
\qquad
E_h \;=\; \int_{24\,\mathrm{h}} h_i \left( T_n - T_{x=L} \right)^{+} dt,
\tag{9}\]
reported as cooling_energy and heating_energy in J/(m²·day).






Note



The average-day DataFrame also carries DeltaTn, the half-width of the comfort zone around \(T_n\) as a function of the daily outdoor temperature swing, following the bioclimatic proposal of Morillón (Morillón-Gálvez et al. 2004) (from ±1.25 °C for swings below 13 °C up to ±3.5 °C for swings above 52 °C). It is provided as data for comfort analyses — e.g. checking how long the free-running \(T_i\) stays inside \(T_n \pm \Delta T_n\) — but solveAC() holds the setpoint at \(T_n\) itself.

title: 1D model: physical problem
text:
The average day
The climate forcing is built from the EPW file for the selected month (Location.meanDay(month, year)), at 1-second resolution:

Outdoor temperature \(T_a\) — the monthly means of the daily minimum and maximum, \(T_{min}\) and \(T_{max}\), are interpolated with the cosine model of Chow & Levermore (2007): the minimum is assumed at sunrise and the maximum at the month’s mean time of daily maximum, both extracted from the EPW.
Irradiances \(I_g\), \(I_b\), \(I_d\) — the month’s hour-by-hour means of global, beam and diffuse horizontal irradiance, interpolated in time to the simulation grid.
Solar position and sunrise — computed with pvlib for the site’s latitude, longitude, altitude and timezone (read from the EPW header).
Comfort quantities — \(T_n\) (Equation 8) and DeltaTn (constant columns).

Tsa() then evaluates Equation 4 on this average day for the system’s tilt, azimuth and absortance, and returns it on the same time grid used by the solvers.

title: 1D model: physical problem
text:
Outputs and units









Result
Mode
Meaning
Units




Ti (DataFrame)
both
Indoor air temperature over the converged day
°C


energy_transfer
solve()
Energy delivered to the indoor air (Equation 7)
J/(m²·day)


cooling_energy
solveAC()
Cooling demand to hold \(T_n\) (Equation 9)
J/(m²·day)


heating_energy
solveAC()
Heating demand to hold \(T_n\) (Equation 9)
J/(m²·day)



Energies are per unit of component surface area, accumulated over one day: divide by \(3600\) for Wh/(m²·day) or by \(3.6\times10^6\) for kWh/(m²·day).

title: 1D model: physical problem
text:
References


ASHRAE. 1997. ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals. SI. American Society of Heating, Refrigerating; Air-Conditioning Engineers.


Barrios, G., J. M. Casas, G. Huelsz, and J. Rojas. 2016. “Ener-Habitat: An Online Numerical Tool to Evaluate the Thermal Performance of Homogeneous and Non-Homogeneous Envelope Walls/Roofs.” Solar Energy 131: 296–304. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.solener.2015.12.017.


Chow, D. H. C., and G. J. Levermore. 2007. “New Algorithm for Generating Hourly Temperature Values Using Daily Maximum, Minimum and Average Values from Climate Models.” Building Services Engineering Research and Technology 28: 237–48.


Holmgren, W. F., C. W. Hansen, and M. A. Mikofski. 2018. “Pvlib Python: A Python Package for Modeling Solar Energy Systems.” Journal of Open Source Software 3 (29): 884. https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.00884.


Humphreys, M. A., and F. J. Nicol. 2000. “Outdoor Temperature and Indoor Thermal Comfort: Raising the Precision of the Relationship for the 1998 ASHRAE Database of Field Studies.” ASHRAE Transactions 106: 485–92.

title: 2D model: non-homogeneous systems
text: Real masonry units are not homogeneous across their width: a concrete hollow block has air cavities between webs, and a joist-and-block (vigueta y bovedilla) roof alternates concrete ribs, filler blocks and cavities. Averaging their properties into an equivalent homogeneous layer misses the physics that matters — heat bridging through the solid webs and the convective/radiative exchange inside the cavities. For these systems EnerHabitat solves the heat transfer on a 2D cross-section of the unit (Barrios et al. 2016).

title: 2D model: non-homogeneous systems
text:
Domain: the repeating cell
Constructive units repeat periodically along the wall or roof, so the domain is a single repeating cell — the block (or the rib-to-rib module) cut across its width and thickness. By periodicity, no heat flows between neighbouring cells: the lateral sides of the cell are adiabatic (symmetry planes).
Axis convention (used by the package and throughout these pages): \(x\) runs across the width of the cell and \(y\) through the thickness, from the outside (\(y = 0\)) to the inside (\(y = e\)), as in the cross-section figures below. Note that the reference paper (Barrios et al. 2016) uses the transposed convention (\(x\) through the thickness).
The cell is a stack in \(y\) — exterior finishes, the non-homogeneous unit, interior finishes — where the unit itself is a 2D patchwork of materials and, possibly, cavities.

title: 2D model: non-homogeneous systems
text:
Governing equations and boundary conditions
Conduction in the solids obeys the two-dimensional extension of the 1D heat equation, with position-dependent properties:
\[
\rho\, c\, \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}
\;=\;
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left( k\, \frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right)
+
\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\!\left( k\, \frac{\partial T}{\partial y} \right),
\tag{1}\]
where \(k(x,y)\), \(\rho(x,y)\) and \(c(x,y)\) take the value of the material occupying each point (rib, filler block, topping, solid fill…). Continuity of temperature and flux at material joints is as in the 1D case.
The boundary conditions close the problem:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y = 0:&\quad h_o \left( T_{sa} - T \right) = -k\, \frac{\partial T}{\partial y}
  && \text{(outdoor, sun–air temperature)}\\[4pt]
y = e:&\quad -k\, \frac{\partial T}{\partial y} = h_i \left( T - T_i \right)
  && \text{(indoor air)}\\[4pt]
x = 0,\ x = W:&\quad \frac{\partial T}{\partial x} = 0
  && \text{(adiabatic sides, periodicity)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
\(T_{sa}\), \(h_o\) and \(h_i\) are exactly those of the 1D model — same average day, same Tsa(). The indoor air \(T_i\) follows the same two solution modes: free-running (lumped air node, now fed by the width-averaged flux from the indoor surface) or air-conditioned (\(T_i = T_n\) constant).

title: 2D model: non-homogeneous systems
text:
Cavity physics (Fill.AIR)
When a cell is an air cavity, three heat-transfer mechanisms act together (Barrios et al. 2016): conduction through the surrounding solids, natural convection of the cavity air, and radiation between the cavity surfaces.

The cavity-air node
The air inside each cavity is modelled as a single lumped node at temperature \(T_h\), exchanging heat by convection with the four cavity walls:
\[
\rho_a\, c_a\, A_{cav}\, \frac{dT_h}{dt}
\;=\;
\oint_{\partial cav} h_c \left( T_w(s) - T_h \right) ds,
\tag{3}\]
where \(A_{cav} = w \cdot d\) is the cavity cross-section (width × depth), the integral runs along the cavity perimeter with \(T_w(s)\) the local wall temperature, and all quantities are per unit length in the out-of-plane direction. In the discrete form the perimeter element \(ds\) becomes the face length (\(\Delta x\) or \(\Delta y\)) of each wall node. The convective coefficient \(h_c\) depends on the cavity orientation.


Convective coefficient: walls vs roofs
For a wall (tilt = 90, vertical cavity) EnerHabitat uses the correlation of Xamán et al. (2005) for cavities of façade elements, as a function of the temperature difference between the two faces across the thickness and the cavity depth \(d\) (m):
\[
h_c \;=\; 0.4005\; \frac{\left| T_{out} - T_{in} \right|^{0.3033}}{d^{\,0.0901}}
\qquad \left[\mathrm{W/m^2\,K}\right].
\tag{4}\]
For a roof (tilt = 0, horizontal cavity) the regime is Rayleigh–Bénard. If the lower face is not hotter than the upper one the air stratifies stably and only conducts, \(h_c = k_{air}/d\). Otherwise convection sets in, described by the correlation of Hollands et al. (1975) for horizontal layers heated from below:
\[
h_c \;=\; \frac{k_{air}}{d}
\left(
1 + 1.44 \left[ 1 - \frac{1708}{Ra} \right]^{+}
  + \left[ \left( \frac{Ra}{5830} \right)^{1/3} - 1 \right]^{+}
\right),
\qquad
Ra = \frac{g\, \beta\, \Delta T\, d^3}{\nu\, \alpha},
\tag{5}\]
where \([\,\cdot\,]^{+}\) keeps the positive part and the air properties are evaluated at ambient conditions (\(k_{air} = 0.0262\) W/m·K, \(\nu = 1.11\times10^{-5}\) m²/s, \(\beta = 1/300\) K⁻¹). Because \(h_c\) depends on the wall temperatures, it is re-evaluated inside the iteration of every time step (see the numerical method).


Radiation between cavity surfaces
The four cavity walls exchange long-wave radiation. The air is non-participating, the surfaces are grey and diffuse with emissivity \(\varepsilon\) (the emissivity parameter, 0.9 by default), and each surface emits at its mean temperature (Incropera et al. 2007). The net exchange between surfaces \(m\) and \(n\) is
\[
q_{m \to n} \;=\; \varepsilon\, \sigma\, F_{mn} \left( T_m^4 - T_n^4 \right),
\tag{6}\]
with \(\sigma\) the Stefan–Boltzmann constant and \(F_{mn}\) the view factor between them. For a rectangular cavity of width \(w\) and depth \(d\) the view factors follow from the crossed-strings method; e.g. between the top wall and one lateral wall, and between the two opposite walls:
\[
F_{u \to r} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left( 1 + \tfrac{d}{w} - \sqrt{1 + \tfrac{d^2}{w^2}} \right),
\qquad
F_{u \to d} = 1 - 2 F_{u \to r}.
\tag{7}\]


Solid fill (Fill.SOLID)
The cavity can instead be filled with a solid material (e.g. an insulating core): the cavity physics switches off and the fill behaves as one more conducting material in Equation 1. Filling with the same material as the shell makes the unit homogeneous — in that limit the 2D solution reduces to the 1D one, which is one of the package’s validation checks (see Validation).

title: 2D model: non-homogeneous systems
text:
Geometries

Hollow-block wall — HollowBlock
A shell of a single material with one cavity per cell; walls only (tilt = 90). The repeating cell takes half a web on each side, so the full web between two cavities is 2·web.






Figure 1: Hollow-block wall cross-section (to scale).




cell width \(W = 2 \cdot \texttt{web} + \texttt{block\_width}\)
thickness \(e = \texttt{cover\_top} + \texttt{cavity} + \texttt{cover\_bottom}\)



Joist-and-block roof — Slab
Roofs only (tilt = 0). Three solid materials — the compression topping, an L-shaped concrete rib (web + foot) at each edge of the cell, and the filler block — plus \(n\) equal cavities, each one with its own lumped air node (Equation 3) and its own \(h_c\).






Figure 2: Joist-and-block roof cross-section (to scale, 3 cavities).




cell width \(W = 2(\texttt{web} + \texttt{foot}) + (n+1)\cdot\texttt{shoulder} + n\cdot\texttt{cavity\_width}\)
thickness \(e = \texttt{topping} + \texttt{cover\_top} + \texttt{cavity} + \texttt{cover\_bottom}\)

The rib’s web rises through the whole section except the top topping_cap of the topping, reproducing the real joist profile.

title: 2D model: non-homogeneous systems
text:
Constraints and outputs

The layers list of a System2D contains exactly one 2D element (HollowBlock or Slab); any other entries are ordinary homogeneous layers (finishes), handled as 1D bands of the cross-section.
The element’s thickness is derived from its geometry, so it is not repeated as a layer thickness.
Orientation is validated: HollowBlock requires tilt = 90, Slab requires tilt = 0.
Outputs are those of the 1D model — Ti, energy_transfer, cooling_energy, heating_energy — expressed per unit of indoor surface area (the width-averaged flux at \(y = e\)), so 1D and 2D results are directly comparable.

title: EnerHabitat
text:
EnerHabitat is a Python package for the thermal simulation of opaque constructive systems (walls and roofs) driven by EPW weather data. It solves the time-dependent heat conduction equation across multi-layer systems — in 1D for homogeneous layers (System) and in 2D for units that are heterogeneous across their width, such as concrete hollow-block walls and joist-and-block (vigueta y bovedilla) roofs (System2D) — and produces indoor temperatures and air-conditioning energy demands for an average day of a chosen month (Barrios et al. 2016).
The model considers a single opaque envelope component: no windows, no ventilation, no infiltration, no internal gains — so any difference in the results is caused by the constructive system alone. Two solution modes are available: free-running (the indoor temperature evolves with the system’s dynamics) and air-conditioned (the indoor temperature is held at a comfort setpoint and the energy demands are reported).

title: EnerHabitat
text:
Installation
pip install enerhabitat        # or: uv add enerhabitat
Requires Python ≥ 3.10. The section inspector plots are an optional extra: pip install enerhabitat[viz].

title: EnerHabitat
text:
Quickstart
EnerHabitat ships no materials: create a materials.ini in your working directory (or point eh.config.file to one) before running anything:
[Adobe]
k   = 0.58    # W/m·K
rho = 1500    # kg/m³
c   = 1480    # J/kg·K
import enerhabitat as eh

eh.config.file = "./materials.ini"           # 1) materials (required)
loc = eh.Location("./epw/example.epw")       # 2) location from an EPW

wall = eh.System(location=loc)               # 3) constructive system
wall.azimuth = 90                            #    east-facing wall
wall.absortance = 0.3
wall.layers = [("Adobe", 0.20)]              #    outside → inside

loc.meanDay(month=5, year=2025)              # 4) average day of May
wall.Tsa()                                   #    sun–air temperature

ti = wall.solve()                            # 5) free-running indoor temperature
print(wall.energy_transfer)                  #    J/(m²·day)

title: Numerical method
text: Both the 1D and the 2D models are solved with the same strategy: an implicit control-volume discretisation of the heat equation (Patankar 1980), advanced in time until the daily solution becomes periodic. This page documents the discretisation, the solution algorithm, the convergence criteria, the differences with the reference paper (Barrios et al. 2016), and the validation record.

title: Numerical method
text:
Discretisation
The domain is divided into control volumes — \(N_x = 200\) through the thickness in 1D (config.Nx); an \(n_x \times n_y = 80 \times 160\) grid (width × thickness) in 2D (config2d). Integrating the heat equation over each volume with a fully implicit (backward-Euler) time scheme gives, per node, an algebraic equation of the form
\[
a_P\, T_P \;=\; a_E\, T_E + a_W\, T_W + a_N\, T_N + a_S\, T_S + b,
\qquad
a_P = \frac{\rho c\, \Delta x \Delta y}{\Delta t} + \sum a_{nb} \;(+\,h\,\Delta s),
\tag{1}\]
where the neighbour coefficients \(a_{nb}\) are the face conductances (only \(E\)/\(W\) exist in 1D), \(b\) carries the previous-time-step term and the boundary sources, and the film coefficients \(h_o\), \(h_i\) enter \(a_P\) and \(b\) at the boundary nodes exactly as the boundary conditions prescribe.
At the face between two control volumes of different materials the conductance uses the harmonic mean of the conductivities — the physically consistent choice for layered media, since it preserves the flux across the interface (Patankar 1980):
\[
k_f \;=\; \frac{2\, k_L\, k_R}{k_L + k_R}.
\tag{2}\]

title: Numerical method
text:
Solution algorithm
1D. The discrete system is tridiagonal, and each time step is solved exactly in one pass of the Tridiagonal Matrix Algorithm (TDMA / Thomas algorithm). No inner iteration is needed.
2D. Each time step is solved line by line: for every row \(j\) (a line across the width) a TDMA solves the \(x\)-direction implicitly, while the \(y\)-neighbour terms use the latest available values (Gauss–Seidel lagging). Sweeps repeat until the mean relative change of the field is below config2d.tol_inner (\(10^{-10}\) by default). The non-linear cavity physics — the convective coefficient \(h_c(\Delta T)\) and the \(T^4\) radiation exchange — is re-evaluated at the start of every sweep, so the converged step is consistent with the cavity state.

title: Numerical method
text:
Indoor-air coupling (free-running mode)
The conduction solver is implicit and therefore unconditionally stable — no time-step restriction comes from the wall itself. The coupling with the indoor air is, however, segregated: each step solves the wall using the indoor temperature of the previous step, and then advances the air node explicitly (forward Euler over the air balance):
\[
T_i^{new} \;=\; T_i \;+\; \mathrm{Fo}_a \left( \overline{T}_{surf} - T_i \right),
\qquad
\mathrm{Fo}_a = \frac{h_i\, \Delta t}{\rho_a\, c_a\, L_a}.
\tag{3}\]
That scalar explicit step is the one piece of the scheme with a stability constraint: \(\mathrm{Fo}_a < 2\) for stability and \(\mathrm{Fo}_a \lesssim 1\) to avoid oscillations. With the fixed \(\Delta t = 10\) s, \(\mathrm{Fo}_a \approx 0.03\) — far inside the stable region. This is why config.dt is locked: a user-enlarged \(\Delta t\) would push the air node toward non-physical behaviour while buying almost no speed (the inner iterations grow to compensate). In the 2D solver the cavity-air nodes \(T_h\) are advanced the same way, with equally small effective Fourier numbers.
In the air-conditioned mode none of this applies: \(T_i\) is a constant setpoint, the scheme is purely implicit, and no stability criterion exists.

title: Numerical method
text:
Convergence to the periodic regime
The boundary forcing (\(T_{sa}\)) is periodic with a 24 h period, so the physical solution of interest is the periodic one. Starting from a uniform field at the neutrality temperature \(\overline{T_n}\), the day is simulated repeatedly — each day starting from the previous day’s final state — until the field stops changing between consecutive days:
\[
C \;=\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\text{nodes}} \left| T^{day+1} - T^{day} \right| \;\le\; C_s.
\tag{4}\]
The tolerance is \(C_s = 5\times10^{-4}\) °C in both solvers (hard-coded in 1D; config2d.tol_day in 2D). The 2D solver additionally caps the iteration at config2d.max_days (60 by default) and reports the number of days actually used in System2D.days — if it equals max_days, the returned solution may not be fully periodic and the tolerance/cap should be revisited.

title: Numerical method
text:
Differences with the 2016 paper
The reference paper describes the online tool Ener-Habitat (v2.2). This package solves the same physical problem but is not a copy of that implementation; the table lists the deliberate differences (each entry verified against the code).

title: Numerical method
text:
Validation
The validation record combines the published validation of the method with the package’s own regression tests:

1D vs EnergyPlus (Barrios et al. 2016): six constructive systems (massive, insulated and mixed), non air-conditioned and air-conditioned, hot month. Maximum differences: indoor temperature 0.5 °C, decrement factor 0.03, lag time 0.4 h, cooling energy 3%, heating energy 4%; both programs rank the systems identically.
2D, filled block: setting the same material everywhere, the 2D solution equals the 1D one (Barrios et al. 2016). The package reproduces this 2D → 1D reduction as a test.
2D, hollow block vs experiment: steady-state heat flux through a concrete hollow-block wall compared with hot-box measurements (Borbón et al. 2010); maximum difference 6.5% (experimental uncertainty ±3.8%) (Barrios et al. 2016).
Package vs legacy code: the 2D solver was ported from the C code of the online tool; tests/golden/ holds golden master dumps of the C solver and the suite (tests/test_eh2d_*.py) checks the port reproduces them, plus geometry, coefficient, single-step, full-day and AC tests.

title: Numerical method
text:
Performance
Each solve is single-threaded, JIT-compiled with numba (the first call in a session pays the compilation cost). In-solver thread parallelism was measured (~1.06× on realistic meshes) and removed as not worthwhile. For parameter sweeps — many independent configurations — parallelise at the process level (multiprocessing, joblib): measured speed-ups are near-linear, ≈6× with 8 processes and ≈10× with 16 on an 18-core machine.
